projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Roy McGinnis was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Good afternoon. Today is November the 7th, 2007. I am Patsy Phillips, the interviewer. I am conducting an oral history interview in Montgomery, Alabama at Prince Institute. I am doing this with Mr. Roy McGinnis, a veteran of World War II, Vietnam and the Korean War. You indicated earlier you would like me to call you Roy.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Please state your name and address for the record.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Roy C. McGinnis, 837 Somerset Drive, S-O-M-E-R-S-E-T, Montgomery, Alabama, 36317.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Let's start off. First you told me you were in the Reserves, correct, or the National Guard?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: No. I was in the Prattville National Guard in 1940. Four or five of our high school students were there. Wasn't nothing to do in Prattville in 1940 in the summertime. And the National Guard were going on a summer camp, so we all signed up. All of us were underage, 17 mostly. But while we were on summer camp in Louisiana, they passed a law that all National Guardsmen would be called in for one year. And we got back from summer camp. And everybody had to make up their mind whether they was going to try to get out of the Guard because they was underage or stay. All five of us wanted to stay because it was exciting going away from home in the service. My father said he could get me out, but I said I wanted to go. So this is how I got started in the Army. It was the 62nd Infantry Brigade Headquarters Company. We went off to Camp Blanding in Florida in November 1940 for active duty. And while in Camp Blanding in Florida, about after six months being in the Army in the Infantry, I decided I wanted to get in the Air Corps where it was a little bit easier. So I transferred to the Army Air Corps in 1941. Came to Maxwell Air Force Base. I wanted to be a pilot, but I didn't have the education. And also I was color-blind. So I signed up for aircraft mechanic school and went to Keesler Field, Mississippi in November of '41. And started aircraft mechanic school the same day the war was declared, December the 7th, 1941. And you asked me what I was doing --

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: What were you doing?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: -- when Pearl Harbor came around. Well, we woke up one Sunday morning, 7th of December. Nobody knew where Pearl Harbor was. The radios were blaring out, "Pearl Harbor bombed," but nobody in the barracks there knew where Pearl Harbor was. This was, I guess, how dumb we were then. [LAUGHTER] But anyway, we finally found out soon. And the next day we all had to turn in our civilian clothes to wear nothing but Army uniforms. And a lot of us just spent our little 21 dollars a month to buy clothes. And we had to get rid of them and give them to the Red Cross or send them home. So I went to aircraft mechanic school for four or five months. And then transferred to Tyndall Field, Florida and was a crew chief on a PT-13 aircraft. Didn't know exactly what I was doing, but they made me a crew chief anyway.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Desperate times, huh?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yeah. While I was at Tyndall Field, Florida, that was the aerial gunners school back in those days, 1942. And I signed up for aerial gunners school, never thinking I would get to go. But one day my name came up on the bulletin board to report to aerial gunner school as a student. I went to aerial gunner school and graduated. By the way, I was still a private from 1940 until '42. Since I had come to aircraft mechanic school, I made staff sergeant at the graduation from aerial gunner school. They made me an aerial gunner instructor. And I was an instructor for about six, seven, eight months and got an aircrew in 1943, B-17 bomber. Transferred to the state of Washington and had our crew training in Washington and Oregon. I was the waist gunner on this B-17. We had a brand-new B-17 when we left Oregon. Picked it up at Seattle, Washington and started on our way across to here. We spent several days in -- I'm trying to think of the name. Anyway, on the East Coast.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So you went from Oregon to the East Coast?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes. With a brand-new B-17 and an inexperienced crew, including the pilot. I was the youngest man on the crew and the pilot was six months older than I was. I was 20 years old at that time. We spent several days waiting for the weather to get right to fly over the ocean. And while we were there, we were getting bored. While we were there in Bangor, Maine -- that's where it was -- waiting for the weather to get right, me and my navigator on the crew who was a second lieutenant -- and I was the staff sergeant. We were sitting in the PX drinking beer one night. And they got ready to close the beer hall. And he said, well, let's go to the officers' club. And I said, No, I can't go to the officers' club, I'm a staff sergeant. He said, Well, I'll fix that. Come to my barracks and I'll give you part of my uniform. And you can get the bombardier shirt and so forth. And I just had just enough beer I guess to not know what I was doing. So me and the navigator showed up at the officers' club. Now, we had a whole training group of officers already there and my pilot and the rest of the officer crew. And I came in as a second lieutenant with bombardier wings on. And I had a ball. [LAUGHTER] My pilot didn't say a thing in the world about it. None of the other officers knew who I was. They knew I was an enlisted man and staff sergeant. Back in those days, they had WAC Corps and nurses and all officer types. And I was having a ball dancing with every one of them. [LAUGHTER] But anyway, after all my crew left, one of my friends and my pilot, another pilot, said, McGinnis, I better get you out of here. And that's when he took me to my plane. And I got up in the nose and went to sleep. The next day, my pilot came by. And since my engineer on my crew saw me in that uniform, he went and told my pilot. My pilot already knew it. But he wanted my pilot to come down and give me dressing down for impersonating an officer. And all my pilot said was, McGinnis, said, don't do that any more. He said, You could have had all of us in the guardhouse. Anyway, that's one of the funny things going overseas. Now, when we got ready to go, the day before, we found out the girls in England -- that's where we were going -- didn't have lipstick or powder or hose of any type. So the word got around if you want to be popular with the girls in England, get all this you could take with you. So we went to the PX and bought lipstick, powder and hose.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Everything a man needs to go to war.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Now, this was in 1943, in September 1943. So we flew this new B-17 overseas and landed in Prestwick, Scotland. And they took our brand-new plane away from us and put us on a train to go to regular training camp in England. And in Bovington, England, it was the training base for all new aircrews coming into England. And we got training there. And while I was there, I met a nurse, a nurse in the hospital there. And I didn't give her none of the hose or lipstick. We just met on the level. And in fact, when I got shot down, all what I had in my baracks, somebody got it. And there was a lot of lipstick and powder and hosiery there. But I found out you didn't really need it. [LAUGHTER] But back in those days, the U.S. Air Force and the Army and all were overriding England. And all the bars and dance halls and all were overrun with American GI's. And the poor English men couldn't compete with the money we got paid. I felt sorry for the English man, but not the English woman. We got ready for combat. And I went and our first mission was Emden, Germany. It's right on the North Sea coast. And they usually give aircrews -- they call it a milk run on the first two or three missions, so they can get used to combat. We lost 10 planes maybe on that mission, which is still a lot of planes. But then I went to Aachen, Germany, for another milk run so-called. And we lost a few planes there. But the third mission, Bremen, Germany, was deep into Germany. And back in those days, we only had fighter cover, Air Force fighter cover, over the coast of France. They had to turn back then because they didn't have enough gas to go all the way into Germany. As soon as you left the middle part of France, all these German fighters started jumping you, some 200 or 300 at the time. And so we went to Bremen, Germany and fought the fighters all the way there. We made the bomb run in Bremen. Before we got to the target area, you could see all these Flak, explosions of Flak in the air before you got there. It was just like a black cloud, about 500 feet thick and I don't know how wide. But we had to fly over that to go to the target. We luckily got through it, our crew did. But they lost many planes that day, 40-something I think. And after that mission, I had made up my mind that I wasn't going to make it through the war. And I wrote my mother and father and told them that. I said, I don't see how I can make 25 missions under the circumstances we're having to fly. And I was scared to death, by the way. But anyway, the next mission was October the 14th, 1943, in Schweinfurt, Germany. And this was called Black Thursday as far as Air Force history goes. On that trip, we lost 62 bombers. And each plane had 10 men on it, so you can see that's 600 and something men. Some of those became Prisoners of War, which I did. We got shot out of formation by Flak and had to drop out of formation. One engine was hit by Flak and the pilot feathered that engine. And what it meant, turned the blade right into the air, so it wouldn't drag on the flight. And had to drop out of formation. Of course, the German fighters jumped us when we fell out of formation and started shooting us in all directions. And another engine caught on fire. And we were flying around 40,000 feet at that time. And the pilot had put it in a dive, trying to put the fire out on the other engine. This he told me later after we were Prisoners of War. I didn't know what he was doing then because I was in the back. And at the time he pulled the plane out of the dive, we were on the treetops. And I had just gotten the emergency door off my side of the plane. And men lined up behind me to push jump out, almost pushed me out. If I hadn't have caught myself in the door, I would have been pushed out on the treetops. But we crash-landed. And she has a picture of that plane. And I guess in about 35, 40 minutes all of us, all 10 men were captured. And there's another story. Me and the navigator -- who were good friends, by the way. You can tell. We went to the officers' club together. Me and the navigator were running across the corn field together. And we hid in the corn field. And on the road right above, we saw this crippled man passing by. And he saw us go in the corn field. And he motioned for us to come, you know. And my navigator wasn't very smart. He thought we might be in Holland or Belgium, but we were still in Germany. He said, Come on, this might be the underground. But we went up to him. And he said, Me Deutschland. And of course, we said, We're Americans. And we was trying to talk. He couldn't speak English. And he got in front of this little building down there. And he grabbed us both by the arm and started yelling. And here come the luftwaffe officer out of the building with the pistol in his hand. And that's how we were captured, us two. But anyway, within 45 or 50 minutes, all of us were in this one room captured. And the German captain there was just raving in English. And nobody could understand what he was saying. And finally, this -- what do you call them? Little town master. What do you call them?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Burgermeister.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: The burgermeister of the town came in. He could speak a little English. All he could do was say, Why are you bombing our women and children? And Roosevelt is an S-O-B. That's about the only English he could speak. Of course, soon after that, they called the men from the little airfield there and took us into a little airfield, a fighter airfield, and put us in different rooms. And while we were there, the fighter pilot that followed our plane all the way down and shot us all the way to the ground almost came by to see how many people were alive from that crew. And, of course, he was surprised. He couldn't speak English either. He was a German. But he was surprised we were all alive. And he traded cigarettes. My pilot still had some cigarettes left. After that, they took us the next day to an interrogation camp in Frankfurt, Germany. And all the prisoners came there for interrogation. And during my interrogation, I was interviewed by a German that could speak perfect English. He was blond, good-looking man. And he spoke better English than I did. And he started asking -- telling me and talking about my name and said I know a clan of McGinnises in Scotland and so on and so froth, and kept on talking a little bit of small-talk. And where did you bomb today or yesterday? What kind of plane were you on? Of course, they gave us a form, the International Red Cross. They had all kind of questions. And I knew we were supposed to fill out the name, rank and serial number only. And I filled out the name, rank and serial number out. And he said, Don't you want your family to know you're a Prisoner of War? I said, Well, they will find out one way or another. I was scared to death, by the way. He said, Fill out the rest of that. I said, No, I'm supposed to fill out my name, rank and serial number. I said, You probably know that. I was wondering what he was going to say. But he started and he said, Where did you bomb? I said, You know where we bombed. He said, Put it down. I put one thing down, Schweinfurt, Germany. And I wrote it on the form S-W-I-N-E-F-O-R-D. I didn't even know how to spell Schweinfurt, Germany. He got so mad, he broke out in German. And he couldn't hold it. He said, You people come over here and can't even spell the name of the target you are bombing. [LAUGHTER] He got really mad. And he said, You know I could have you shot. You don't even have an I.D. tag. But he didn't. I went on out and he went on to the rest of my crew. After that, some days later we stayed in that little interrogation camp four or five days. And they started shipping us out to different prison camps. We got down into the railroad station in Frankfurt and waiting to get on a train. And we saw so many different groups of Americans under guard, we thought the whole Air Force had got shot down. But anyway, there was a nice-looking German. The girls looked nice. They had good-looking clothes and everything. This one good-looking German girl, I thought she smiled at me. And I winked at her. [LAUGHTER] She come up and spit in my face. I think she did this because she knew guards were there and there was some of them watching her. But she started and all these people started -- what they was saying in German, I don't know. Pretty soon we had a crowd of civilians around about to take me under. And the guard finally pushed us into -- and they took the guns down on the civilians. And we got in boxcars finally, thank goodness, because I was really scared. We rode the boxcar three or four days and went down to Stalag 17B which is located in Krems, Austria, right on the Danube. And this is where Stalag 17 is located. And we went there. And this camp had been a Russian -- had been a camp for Russian workers that the Germans had captured, so it was full of lice, worn down on all kind of stuff there. But we all went there and all the Americans were already coming in fast. And by the way, at the end of that war, there was 4500 American gunners in that camp. That's 4,500 -- which is a lot of planes that got shot down. But that was the end of the war. But anyway, we got to camp and got set up in whatever way you can get set up. We had people already there showing us what to do. And you're going to have to ask me some questions now.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I keep rambling.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: No, no. I'm enjoying this. How were you treated there? What did you eat?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Well, the treatment was better than I expected. I don't know whether you know it or not, but the Germans during World War II, they did honor the Geneva Convention to some degree, especially for the Americans and the English. That meant they had to go by certain treatment of Prisoners of War. Now, what they did in that, they gave us what they had. They didn't have nothing really. But they treated us good in this respect. They let the International Red Cross come in with food parcels once a week. And we got clothing from the International Red Cross, which the American government furnished through Switzerland. They let that happen. But all during the time that was happening, the Germans got their cut out of it.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: But like I say, we were first guarded by the luftwaffe men, luftwaffe personnel. That was a German Air Force personnel. This old captain in our compound must have been 65 or 70 years old. And he had been in World War I. And he was a very nice gentleman, he seemed to be. He pleaded for us to do well when we went out to roll call every morning. But anyway, initially, we had plenty to eat. The Germans gave us very poor rations of food. Now, let me describe one of these Red Cross parcels for you. It was about 12 pounds of food. It had a can of coffee, powdered milk, sugar, a little can of margarine, a can of salmon, sea rations, five packs of cigarettes, two D-bars which is chocolate bars, concentrated chocolate bars and such similar things as that. We got that once a week, to start with. And that was supposed to last you with whatever the Germans gave you every day. Since we had coffee in our parcels, the Germans gave us hot water for your breakfast. You used your coffee and whatever you had in the parcel to eat. Noontime, we got some sort of soup, cabbage or rutabaga soup. It was tasty, but it was full of worms or whatever else really they would gather. And 1/4 per man of a hard loaf of bread, to start with. At night, we had a couple of potatoes and maybe sometime a piece of some kind of meat. I never could identify it. I guess it was horse meat. I think it was. Anyway, that went on for a good while. But after the war kept going on and the Americans started bombing all the targets and the railroads and the roads, the Red Cross parcels couldn't get through. And so you had to start depending on the Germans to feed you, which was toward the end of the war. It was terrible because they just didn't have anything. The guards ate about the same thing we did as far as food goes. But what do we do to keep ourselves happy? In my barracks -- there was 150 men in the barracks, I think. We came from all different places in the United States. We talked about everything from the Civil War to your girlfriend or what's happening in the war. This is how we entertained ourself, to start with. And later on, the International YMCA through Switzerland sent in musical instruments, baseball equipment, softball equipment, different books and things like that. And the camp was very well organized by Americans. And we had a staff sergeant who was in charge of the camp, and he spoke German well. And we were all organized under our American control. We didn't have much control there, but under our American control. And the Germans were always supposed to go to our camp leader for whatever he wanted us to do. Anything was supposed to go through them and explain what he wanted. Anyway, in that respect, it was not bad. Of course, as the war went on, suffering began. People were losing weight, not much to eat. And we were wondering if we were ever going to get out of there. One thing about being a Prisoner of War, you didn't know what was going to happen the next day. Eventually, they took the luftwaffe guards off our camp and replaced them with the Russian-Germans that had come back from the Russian front who had been wounded and got back. And they were mean. They just tried to make you mad or whatever. But they were just mean people. But anyway, we got through that. But we did have a pretty good organization as far as music. We had a lot of musicians. Out of 4500 Prisoners of War, we had some musicians that had been musicians in a well-known orchestra here and there. We got together and we formed an orchestra. They got a theater and stuff from the International YMCA, also. We formed an acting company. And they called it the Cardboard Playhouse, but they started putting on plays. As crude as it was, it was very good. And even the Germans, the German higher-ups, they liked it. They came down, too. And by the way, the camp where we were, we were 4500. They had about 30,000 different prisoners in this whole camp. And it was made up of Russians, all types of European nationalities that the Germans had used to work. We didn't have any Jews there, by the way. And I'll tell you about the thing. When I got on this boxcar in Frankfurt -- and I'm going back. I looked out the little window we had had in the boxcar and saw all these cattle cars there with women, men and children. You know what a cattle car is. You can see through them. And I asked the guard, What are they? He said in poor English, They are workers going to work camp. They are going to work camp. I didn't know that they were Jews then. They were on their way to be annihilated then. I didn't know that. And you know that they killed millions of Jews over there. But I found out later after I was in that camp what they were going to do. Okay. October, survived the first winter. Summer, was glad to be there. We put all our mattresses out and got the bugs out. In the summertime, we could lay them out and it was full of all kind of bugs. And so was people, if they didn't -- especially hairy men and hairy people, they got all kind of bugs. It was always the threat of typus in the camp. T-Y-P-U-S. It's a disease. It's a fever. Typus fever. I think that's the way you spell it. Anyway, summertime was good. We could get outside and get rid of the bugs and go around. We got a bath, a hot bath about every three months. They would take us up to I guess a big compound where they had showers and everything. They cut on the water about five minutes. You'd soap up, and that's it. That's the bath you got, hot bath you got. These barracks, they didn't have but one spigot in the middle of the barracks for 200 and something people and the water come on at certain times of the day. I take it back. They had five or six spigots. One spigot was a showerhead, but it only stayed on one hour a day or something like that. Cold water, no hot water. Ask me some questions.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Okay. You were talking about the men with their hair, the bugs in there. How did you cut your hair?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: The Germans when we first got captured, there was one of the deals. They shaved your head. They shaved your head so they could identify you as a prisoner of some sort. All prisoners had shaved heads. Now, as we went on through the prison camp, time went on, they took us up to -- when they got you a bath, they shaved your head again. Now, the Americans are pretty sharp people. Some of them didn't want their heads shaved. So they take this margarine and put it in their hair and put sand in their hair. And when they run the clippers in their head, it tore them up.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: But the Germans got so mad, one of them whenever they did it, and pretty soon there was no more clippers. So we all grew hair.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: But were there any other men on the airplane -- the 10 men on the airplane, were they in the camp with you? Were they pretty close to you?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Of the six enlisted men and five of us was in the same camp. One engineer, he went to another camp by himself because he had a broken leg. He had a broken leg. And all the crew members were with us in the same camp.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Now, these spigots of water turned on an hour or two a day, was there a rush to get to it?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes. You can imagine if you had any clothes you wanted to wash -- and we didn't have many clothes at all but we did get some from the International Red Cross. But you had to wash your clothes and whether you wanted to wash yourself. It's fighting to get in there. Sometimes you would get up in the middle of the night, hoping to be in there when it came on.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Was that for your drinking, also?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So you had to get your water that one time.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I think I'd forget about my clothes.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Most people did. They were eager to get the drinking water and all. So the clothes were washed, what little clothes you had. You didn't have no soap most of the time. You had some hard stuff they gave us. Now, we talked about parcels. Eventually, my family, my mother and father found out after three or four months that I was a Prisoner of War. I was first listed as Missing in Action for about three months. And then they finally found out and the International Red Cross finally notified the government who had become prisoners. And after that time, they found out I was a Prisoner of War. Back in those days, your parents or whoever was allowed to send you -- in the United States a package every three months or something, a package or a letter. And I didn't get my first letter from my mother and daddy for I guess it was about 14 months.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: How long were you a Prisoner of War?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Nineteen months. But I was talking about the little nurse I met in Bovington, England. And I got one from her before I got one from my mother and father. She wrote to the International Red Cross in Switzerland and found out I was a Prisoner of War. This young lady, from the short time we met, we were in love. And I was going to meet her family the next time I got on leave. But I didn't ever get on leave again. And she wrote me that first letter.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Were you able to write letters?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: We got three or four form letters a month. Little form letters about that long you could write. And it went through a censor. And whatever you said, if it was anything bad, it would knock it out or wouldn't send it. You could say I'm doing well or I'm here or whatever. And then we got some parcels from home after about 12 or 14 months that they sent and they were allowed to send from home. Usually by that time, everybody was hungry all the time. We usually got socks and gloves, and everybody wanted food. But anyway, they didn't know what to send. Okay. I'm getting carried away on this stuff.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So you could not write and say I need food?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: No. You couldn't write about conditions in the camp. You couldn't tell them anything. Now, the International Red Cross came every three months. Officials came to inspect the camps. Under the Geneva Convention, they could do this. They came and they made up the reports of the conditions and the prisoners. And they sent it back to our government. That's how they found out what was going on. This is the report I'm going to give you of the Military Intelligence Service, War Department. And it covers everything in here, but recreation, religion. By the way, religion -- we had a chaplain in there that was captured in North Africa in the Army. And I understand he could have been released as a Prisoner of War, but he chose to be there and serve the prisoners. And that was the only religious man we had in the camp. And of course, he gave service to everybody. And we had a medical officer, a major. No use giving the name. He was captured in North Africa. He was a surgeon. A dentist captured in North Africa. And this chaplain was captured in North Africa. So they were there and they furnished them a little place to see Prisoners of War, but they didn't have nothing to work with. They had to just give them some pills, whatever they had, whatever the International Red Cross gave them for pills. But they were there, too, also. But they have no authority in the camp. And the staff sergeant in charge of the camp was the camp leader. Now, when we were released later on and these officers took charge under the Americans and they took over as the -- I'll get to that in a minute. Okay. In April 1945, the Russians were coming through Vienna. We were about 40 miles from Vienna. And the Germans were retreating and all the way back. And for some reason, the Germans decided to take us out of the camp and march us back toward the allies, the Americans and the British. And they started marching us out of the camp in 500 groups, giving you about three or four hours apart to leave the camp. So we marched for 18 days, 180 kilometers. I think that equals out to about 100 miles or so. But we marched from Krems, Austria to Braunau, Austria in the forest. B-R-A-U-N-A-U, Austria. That's where Hitler was born, by the way. They stopped us right in the forest, no food, no cover. Everybody tore down the bark off of trees. And we stayed there about four or five days waiting for the allies to catch up and meet us. And finally, we got liberated by Patton's Army. And this was a glorious day, by the way. Glorious day.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I imagine.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Now, during that time, Roosevelt died. In April, Roosevelt died while we were on that march. The Germans started going around and dancing around and says, Roosevelt kaput, like that's going to change something, you know. And that's how we found out Roosevelt had died. It was kind of sad because Roosevelt would have been the president about 12 years or something, I think, something like that. But that's how we found out that Roosevelt died. It didn't change anything in the war. Now, Hitler had tried to use all Prisoners of War during this time as a bargaining chip. Says I'll kill all Prisoners of War if you don't give us better terms on surrender. And we didn't find that out until later, thank goodness.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I would have been scared to death. But I found out later that he was threatening to kill all Prisoners of War if he didn't get better terms. At least, they didn't do that. People under him didn't. Anyway, we were liberated. And we transferred finally to France, Camp Lucky Strike, France.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Camp Lucky Strike?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: They named them after cigarettes. I think they had Camp Camel. But it was Camp Lucky Stripe. By the way, cigarettes were valuable in those days. Even at five packs of cigarettes, we could bargain with the guards to get a little bit of onions or whatever kind of food they had in excess. Very valuable. We used to gamble with them. Me and me partner, one of the radio men on my crew, we went together and pooled our parcels. We would take one parcel to gamble with and use one parcel. When I talk about gambling, we played cards, poker.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So you had cards?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yeah, we had cards. Eventually had cards through the International YMCA. So sometimes we ate very poorly, sometimes we ate good.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Depending on lady luck.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: But anyway, I'm getting out of whack here. Camp Lucky Strike and camps were set up all over France to take care of the prisoners. And they knew we had hundreds of thousands of them. And they fed us. And you could have all the food you wanted to eat any time you wanted to. They had eggnog with no alcohol in it sitting all over the camp with big -- you could go and drink all the eggnog. They wanted you to gain weight. By the way, I didn't lose but about 15 pounds, I think.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Is that because you were a good gambler?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Is that because you were a good gambler and you won food?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: No, it's just because that was the way it was. I was lucky. Some of them lost a lot of weight. Then we finally went and got put on the ship and came back to the United States. And I got seasick when I got in the Le Havre. Le Havre, France was the harbor there. I was seasick after I got out in the harbor. I was seasick before we even took off. But I was sick all the way to New York, and seasick. But it took us about five and a half days to get to New York Harbor. This is where we were released to go home to the different camps.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: How did you get home then? Surely, they provided transportation.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes. They had it pretty well organized. When they found out where you lived and you went to a certain base in the United States -- I went to Camp Fort Dix in Philadelphia. From there, I was supposed to catch a troop train down to North Carolina where my folks lived at that time. I found out the quicker -- if I told them I lived in Philadelphia, I got released in Philadelphia. And now, my radio man on my crew lived in Philadelphia. And they told us in the Camp Lucky Strike that according to where you lived is where you have to ride the poop train to. So I told them my address was the same as my radio man. That means I got released as soon as I got to Philadelphia. Didn't have to ride the poop train all the way to North Carolina, which probably would have been delayed. Now, my family lived in North Carolina in one town. And they had moved about 200 miles to another town in North Carolina. I didn't know it. And, of course, when I got to Philadelphia, everybody went wild over living again. And I spent two or three days in Philadelphia trying to catch a train home. I was having too good a time. But my folks didn't have a phone and I sent telegrams to my old address. Every day I said I'm going to catch this train home. The man in Rockingham, North Carolina sent the telegram to Burlington, North Carolina where they knew my father went. They knew him because I was the first Prisoner of War in that county. So they came down to Rockingham, North Carolina and stayed in a hotel three days waiting for me to come in, my brother, my sister and my mother and father. And they met every train coming in. They didn't know when I was coming in. I just said I'm coming. And on that third day, I came in and I didn't know they had moved.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So how old was your brother and sister?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: My brother was 10 years younger than I and my sister is three years younger.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: There had to be some kind of celebration.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: It was, it was a celebration, yes. And I went on 90 days temporary duty at home and finally got released from the service in October of 1945. And in the meantime, my family moved back to Alabama. And I married 1946 a girl from Sylacauga, Alabama, where I was born. And jobs were very poor in that town and hard to find. So he came back in the service in 1947. Came back to Maxwell Air Force Base in 1947. Came back in as a staff sergeant. Now, do you want to go through the whole --

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: It's what you want to talk about.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Well, I'm not going into detail. When I came back, I was an aircraft mechanic, which I had got trained before at Maxwell Air Force Base for two or three years. I finally got able to get out of the mechanic field and into personnel, thank God. And went to the Korean War, had good assignments all during the Korean War. Didn't go to Korea. Stationed at several universities for ROTC and different places like that. Vietnam came. I got picked for Vietnam. Went to Phu Cat, P-H-U capital C-A-T, Air Base in South Vietnam for one year. That was in 1966. And I came back in October 1967 and put in for retirement from the Air Force. I retired at Columbus Air Force Base, Mississippi in 1968.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: What did you do in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I was a personnel sergeant major of the 37th Combat Support Group. And by the way, I had made chief master sergeant by that time.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Was there any problems when you came home from protestors?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: In Vietnam, yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Different than when you came back from World War II.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: You got treated terribly when you came back home in San Francisco. I came home and I couldn't believe what I was seeing, how the protestors were waiting for people getting off the plane coming back from Vietnam and saying you've been over there killing women and children. And it was terrible. I just didn't expect that. And after that, I went to work for the State of Alabama in the State Department of Veteran Affairs. And I worked with the State Department of Veteran Affairs for 15 years. And during the last four years of that term, I was the director in that department, State Department of Veteran Affairs here in Montgomery. And so I've been retired from that since 1981.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Is there any unusual story or funny thing that really sticks out in your mind about all of your experiences?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Well, I did get a chance to meet Clark Gable.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Well, that's good.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I don't know if you want to go into that or not.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: While I was the air gunner instructor, Clark Gable came to Tyndall Field, Florida. He just graduated from OCS in Miami. And they were running him through a fast course there. And my roommate then -- I was the staff sergeant. Said my sister and my girlfriend is coming here. They want to get a chance to see Clark Gable. And he said, Would you date my sister? He showed me a picture and she was a good-looking girl. I said sure. So they came and spent three days. And we were trying to see Clark Gable. Couldn't see him on the base. And the last day of the stay here was Saturday. And we were down in Panama City up on the roof of the Dixie Sherman Hotel. And we were having some drinks. And they were all sad because they didn't get to see Clark Gable. And who do you think came in? Clark Gable came in with a base commander and with all this entourage he had following him around and sat down. Of course, immediately my girlfriend said, Go get his autograph. I said, I can't do that. I said, I'm a staff sergeant. He's sitting there with the base commander. And she kept on. Of course, I had two more beers. [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: They get you in trouble, those beers.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: And she kept on and I said okay. So I went up and approached the big table there. They had a big, round table with all this entourage sitting there. And I approached the lieutenant, saluted him and stood in front of him and saluted. And he stood up. Nice guy, real nice guy. He stood up and said, What can I do for you, sergeant? I said, my girlfriend here is from Georgia. And she's been waiting three days to see you and she would like to have your autograph. Well, you could see the base commander and I could feel his eyes peering through me, but I didn't even look at him. He said, you know, Sergeant, if I start signing autographs, I'll never get out of here. I said, well, lieutenant, I won't let another soul come up here. So he said, okay. He signed that autograph. And I saluted and walked off. And my girlfriend was as happy as she could be. I guess she's still got that if she's still living. There's a lot of good things that happened like that. I can't go into all of them, but I can tell you all kind of stories.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: That's what makes it interesting.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: But one point I didn't cover, I was married for 41 years to my first wife. She died of cancer. And soon afterwards, I got married to another lady here in Montgomery. And after five years of marriage, she got killed in an automobile accident in Prattville. And after that, sometime after that, not long after that, I just couldn't come home at night. I had a big house in Prattville and I couldn't come home at night. I was lonesome. So I prayed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: It worked out. It all worked out.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You got captured by another German, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I prayed for one more Christian wife. And within two days I had called the church I belonged to in Prattville, which I never did attend, and asked them for -- did they have a group of -- what do you call it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Support group.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: A support group. They said they didn't have one and they referred me to the First Baptist Church over here in Montgomery. And they didn't have one either. But they referred me to Frazer. And I called the lady at Frazer and I know her today. In fact, we went to the ballroom dancing class together, not with each other. She said you'll be welcome over here. And I came over here one night, Tuesday night. She had lost her husband in the same month of my wife died in an automobile accident. She came that first time.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Now, this is things I probably wouldn't do if I don't think the Lord is guiding me.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You didn't have a couple of beers, did you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Okay, good.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: It was about 25, 30 women there in this support group and three men. So you go around the table and they say how you miss your spouse and what you've been doing for the last few days. Of course, since I had lost two wives, I had the feeling that I was kind of a veteran at that. I told them how I missed my spouses. And then I said, "I'm here looking for a wife." [LAUGHTER] I normally wouldn't do that.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Well, all those women's mouths flew open. And some of them said -- I can see what you are thinking, you crazy fool. One woman spoke up on the end and said, I have a house on the lake, do you want to go fishing? She just didn't look like I wanted to go with her. [LAUGHTER] Now, Hilda was there. And her daughter had just had a new baby. Her daughter did. And she's looking at all these pictures at the table in front of us. And I didn't think she was interested at all. But she was she told me later. [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: I didn't want to be pushy.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: But nothing happened. The next week, we came and the same thing. And everybody went around the table again. And they said, What you doing? I said, Well, I'm going broke buying different women dinner every night. And nothing happened after that. But that was Memorial Day 1993 -- or right before Memorial Day. I went down to see my sister on Memorial Day in Florida. And I came back and I had a message on my phone from her, Hilda. And she said, What you doing on this hot Saturday afternoon? [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: I didn't know he was going to bring that up.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You did not know this was going to the Library of Congress, did you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Erase that, please.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Well, it's the truth. Then we made a date to meet at the next meeting. And that's where we had our first date. And soon after that, within six months later, we got married.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Neat.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I can go on forever, how we went on our honeymoon and how we got married quick.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: We better stick to the war. I have some pictures and it's of the airplane. And I thank you so much. Now, did all of these men make it through?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: All of them made it through. One guy with a broken leg.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Would you put on record -- I know. But would you tell them how you got this picture?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: This is just amazing.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Let me have a copy there.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I've got copies of several things here. This is the copy of something else that someone gave me. There you go. That one and this one.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: 50 years later, 50 years after being a Prisoner of War, my pilot belonged to the 96th Bomb Group Association. He got a newsletter in February 1995 that had an article in it which I'm going to read to you. And this article said for French Historian -- you don't have to copy this down if you don't want to. It came from a French historian by the name of Patrick Baunann, B-A-U-N-A-N-N. He said I'm researching American planes which crashed in Alsace, A-L-S-A-C-E, during World War II. I found a picture of the 96th 339th aircraft number 4230709, which crashed 14 October 1943 Schweinfurt mission. Says, Can you tell me about the history of this plane and put me in contact with the survivors? And the editor's note says, To whom this letter -- you don't need to know that. What happened, my pilot is a member. He got the bulletin and wrote to the bulletin. And Coles Goodner was listed. Just put that in there and I'll quit trying to read it.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: After 50 years to see the airplane and all the memories.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You spent just about all of your time as a guest of the German government as a Prisoner of War.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: During the war, yes. 19 months, that's most of it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: That's a nice way of putting it.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Yeah. I can't think of anything else. Do you attend any reunions? Do you see any of the guys?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Yes. We belong to the 2nd Schweinfurt, it's 2nd Schweinfurt.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Do you know how to spell it now?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: S-C-H-W-E-I-F-U-R-T.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: That's the one they got mad that you couldn't spell it?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: No. I belonged to the 2nd Schweinfurt Memorial Association. This is made up of all the flyers that made the Schweinfurt raid in 1943 and went on the Black Thursday raid in 1943. Not necessarily the ones that got shot down, but the ones that didn't get shot down. The Germans had an association of Flak gunners, AK-AK gunners. You know what Flak is. AK-AK gunners that shoots at the planes. Call them Flak gunners, F-L-A-K gunners. All these men were high school students then. When they had an air-raid, all the male high school students had to report to a gunnery station and pass up the shells to put in the guns. They formed an association of Flak gunners. Then sometime in 1993, they formed and met and joined our association, the 2nd Schweinfurt Memorial Association.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Did you get to meet any of them?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Oh, yes. I met them several times. I've been to Germany once. They had the meeting this last October there in Germany in Schweinfurt. And we didn't go because I had been before.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I know you may be tired.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I'm not tired.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: How did you wind up in America?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Okay. You want to tell her or you want me to?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Go ahead. You tell her. You're doing good.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Hilda was married to a -- she has a whole another story, but we ain't going to go into that. She met a German sergeant major.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: American sergeant major.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: American sergeant major in Iran in 1960. Back in those days, the shah was in charge of Iran and we had troops over there. And her daddy was an engineer. And he had been sent from Germany to build electrical --

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: They brought electricity into the town. They didn't have any.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Anyway, she worked for an American hospital.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: In Shiraz.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Shiraz. And that's where she met this American sergeant major. Bless him. I'm glad he brought you home. [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You may have had to go fishing with that woman.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: They got married and came to the States in 1960. Of course, she lost him in 1993, same time I lost my wife. I've already told you how we met.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: Now, you were in Germany during all of this.

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: Yes, I was in Berlin.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: You were like six years old; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: I was this high, yes.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: So you never knew all the planes flying over, one of them --

sp.speaker: Mrs. McGinnis
sp.p: I recall some of it.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: What if you knew I was going to marry that man someday?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Thank goodness, we never bombed Berlin where she lived. You can say it this way. You can say it two ways. I got even with the Germans, I married one. [LAUGHTER] Or I got captured twice by the Germans. I'm still captured by one.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I can't think of anything else. Anything you want to add?

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: I thank you for doing this.

sp.speaker: Patsy Phillips
sp.p: I want to tell you how much we appreciate what you do.

sp.speaker: Roy McGinnis
sp.p: Thank you very much. I'm glad I'm still alive to receive that thanks. I'll be 85 in January.
